column9: Match each vocabulary word to its meaning.
column14: Gene :: A segment of DNA that codes for a specific trait
column15: Allele :: A different version of the same gene, like T or t
column16: Trait :: A specific characteristic, like eye color
column17: Heredity :: The passing of traits from parents to offspring
column18: Genetics :: The scientific study of heredity
column28: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a trait, and alleles are the different versions of that gene (T and t). A trait is the characteristic itself, like eye color. Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring, and genetics is the scientific study of heredity.
column29: Words ending in -ics (like physics) name a field of study. Also notice that some meanings use another word from the list; use those links to connect the words.

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Genotype :: The combination of alleles an organism has, like Bb
column15: Phenotype :: The physical trait that is expressed, like brown fur
column16: Dominant allele :: Shows whenever it is present; written as a capital letter
column17: Recessive allele :: Shows only with two copies; written as a lowercase letter
column18: Probability :: The likelihood that an event will occur
column28: Your genotype is your allele combination (Bb), and your phenotype is what actually shows (brown fur). A dominant allele (capital letter) shows whenever it is present, and a recessive allele (lowercase letter) shows only when there are two copies. Probability is how likely an event is, often written as a percent or a fraction.
column29: Sort the meanings on the right: which examples are written in letters, and which describe something you could observe? Then ask which kind of allele can stay hidden.

column9: In horses, a black coat (**B**) is dominant over a chestnut coat (**b**). A horse has the genotype **Bb**. What type of genotype is this?
column28: Bb has two different alleles, so it is heterozygous (a hybrid). Homozygous dominant would be BB, homozygous recessive would be bb, and purebred means two identical alleles, which Bb does not have.
column29: Are the two letters the same or different?

column9: In tomato plants, red fruit (**R**) is dominant over yellow fruit (**r**). A homozygous recessive, yellow-fruited plant has the genotype ___.
column28: Homozygous recessive means two copies of the recessive (lowercase) allele: rr. RR is homozygous dominant and Rr is heterozygous, and both of those plants have red fruit.
column29: Homozygous means two of the same allele. Which letter stands for yellow?

column9: In corn, purple kernels (**P**) are dominant over yellow kernels (**p**). What is the phenotype of a kernel with the genotype **Pp**?
column16: Light purple, a blend of both colors
column28: Purple (P) is dominant, so one P is enough to make the kernel purple, and the recessive yellow allele is hidden. A light purple blend or a half-and-half kernel is not how a dominant–recessive trait works.
column29: In a dominant–recessive trait, what happens to the recessive allele when a dominant allele is present?

column9: Two parents who both show the dominant phenotype can have a child who shows the recessive phenotype.
column28: True. Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) both show the dominant trait, but each can pass on the hidden a. One box in four is aa, so 25% of their children are expected to show the recessive trait.
column29: Try a Punnett square for two heterozygous parents. Can any box get two recessive alleles?

column9: Gregor Mendel, the "father of modern genetics," did his famous heredity experiments with which organism?
column28: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk (1822–1884), did his famous heredity experiments with pea plants and is called the father of modern genetics. Fruit flies (Thomas Hunt Morgan), mice, and corn became important genetics organisms for later scientists.
column29: Mendel was a monk who ran his experiments in his monastery's garden.

column9: What is the name of the chart that shows all the possible combinations of alleles that can result from a genetic cross?
column28: A Punnett square shows every allele combination that can come from a cross. A pedigree tracks a trait through a family, a karyotype is a picture of chromosomes, and a genotype is one organism's allele combination.
column29: It is the grid you fill in with one allele from each parent.

column9: Mendel crossed purebred round-seed plants with purebred wrinkled-seed plants. What are the **offspring** of this first cross called?
column28: The purebred parents are the P (P1) generation, and their offspring are the F1 generation. When F1 plants are crossed with each other, their offspring are the F2 generation.
column29: F stands for filial, from the Latin word for son or daughter.

column9: In guinea pigs, black fur (**B**) is dominant over white fur (**b**). Which answer lists **every** genotype that gives a guinea pig black fur?
column28: Black is dominant, so any guinea pig with at least one B has black fur: BB (homozygous dominant) and Bb (heterozygous). "BB only" misses that one B is enough, and bb is the only genotype that gives white fur.
column29: How many dominant alleles does it take to show the dominant trait?

column9: In cats, short hair (**L**) is dominant over long hair (**l**). A purebred short-haired cat (**LL**) is crossed with a long-haired cat (**ll**). What percent of the kittens are expected to have short hair? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: LL × ll. Every box gets one L from the short-haired parent and one l from the long-haired parent, so all 4 boxes are Ll. Ll shows the dominant trait, so 100% of the kittens have short hair (and all are heterozygous).
column29: The LL parent can only pass on one kind of allele. What does every kitten get from that parent?

column9: How many alleles for each gene does a parent pass on to each of its offspring?
column15: None, if the allele is recessive
column28: Each parent passes on only one allele for each gene, because the two alleles separate when eggs and sperm form (Mendel's Law of Segregation). The offspring ends up with two alleles, one from each parent. A recessive allele is passed on just like a dominant one.
column29: The offspring has two alleles for each gene. How many came from each parent?

column9: If you know an organism's phenotype, you always know its exact genotype.
column28: False. A dominant phenotype can come from two genotypes (AA or Aa), so you can't always tell which one from the outside. Only the recessive phenotype tells you the genotype for sure (aa).
column29: Think of a tall pea plant. Could it have more than one genotype?

column9: An organism with two identical alleles for a trait, such as **TT** or **tt**, is ___ for that trait.
column28: Two identical alleles (TT or tt) means homozygous, also called purebred or true-breeding. Two different alleles (Tt) would be heterozygous, or hybrid.
column29: Homo- means same; hetero- means different.

column9: What is the difference between a **monohybrid** cross and a **dihybrid** cross?
column14: A monohybrid cross uses one parent; a dihybrid cross uses two parents
column15: A monohybrid cross uses purebreds; a dihybrid cross uses hybrids
column16: A monohybrid cross tracks one trait; a dihybrid cross tracks two traits
column17: A monohybrid cross makes one offspring; a dihybrid cross makes two
column28: Mono- means one and di- means two: a monohybrid cross follows one trait, and a dihybrid cross follows two traits at once (like height and seed color). Both kinds of crosses use two parents, either can involve purebreds or hybrids, and both predict many offspring.
column29: Look at the prefixes: mono- and di-.

column9: In cattle, the polled (hornless) allele (**P**) is dominant over the horned allele (**p**). Jacob crosses two heterozygous polled cattle (**Pp × Pp**). What percent of the calves are expected to have horns? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Pp × Pp → PP, Pp, Pp, pp. Only pp has horns, which is 1 of 4 boxes = 25%. The other 75% are polled (PP or Pp).
column29: Horned is the recessive phenotype. How many of the 4 boxes have two recessive alleles?

column9: In tomato plants, red fruit (**R**) is dominant over yellow fruit (**r**). Two heterozygous plants are crossed (**Rr × Rr**). What is the expected **genotype ratio**?
column28: Punnett square: Rr × Rr → RR, Rr, Rr, rr, which is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr (a 1:2:1 genotype ratio). "3 red : 1 yellow" is the phenotype ratio, not the genotype ratio, and 3 RR : 1 rr and 2 RR : 2 rr leave out the two Rr boxes.
column29: A genotype ratio counts the letter combinations in the boxes, not the colors.

column9: In a breed of dog, a black nose (**N**) is dominant over a brown nose (**n**). Addy crosses two heterozygous black-nosed dogs (**Nn × Nn**). The expected **phenotype ratio** (black : brown) is ___.
column20: 3:1|3 : 1|3: 1|3 :1|3 to 1|3-1|75:25|75 : 25|75%:25%|3 black : 1 brown|3 black:1 brown|3 black to 1 brown|75% : 25%|75%: 25%|75% :25%|75: 25|75 :25|3 black: 1 brown|3 black :1 brown|3 black to 1 brown nose
column28: Punnett square: Nn × Nn → NN, Nn, Nn, nn. Three boxes have at least one N (black) and one box is nn (brown), so the phenotype ratio is 3 black : 1 brown, or 3:1. The genotype ratio would be 1:2:1.
column29: Fill in the 4 boxes, then count black-nosed (at least one N) against brown-nosed (nn).

column9: Storm crosses a heterozygous purple-kernel corn plant (**Pp**) with a yellow-kernel corn plant (**pp**). Purple (**P**) is dominant. Out of 240 kernels, about how many are expected to be **yellow**?
column28: Punnett square: Pp × pp → Pp, Pp, pp, pp. Half of the boxes are pp (yellow), so about 1/2 × 240 = 120 yellow kernels. (A common mistake is to use the 3:1 ratio from two heterozygous parents. That would give about 180 purple and 60 yellow, but here only one parent is heterozygous.)
column29: Find the fraction of boxes that are pp, then take that fraction of 240.

column9: A farmer's black bull could be **BB** or **Bb** (black, **B**, is dominant over red, **b**). Which cross would best reveal the bull's genotype?
column14: Cross him with a black cow (BB)
column15: Cross him with a heterozygous black cow (Bb)
column16: Look closely at the shade of his black coat
column17: Cross him with a red cow (bb)
column28: This is a test cross: cross the unknown with a homozygous recessive (bb) animal. A red cow can only give b, so if the bull is Bb, about half the calves should be red; if every calf is black, he is probably BB. A BB cow would make every calf black no matter what, a Bb cow would show red calves less often (only 1/4 of the time), and the shade of his coat doesn't show his genotype.
column29: For each cow, ask: if the bull were Bb, could any red calves appear, and how often?

column9: A purebred purple-flowered pea plant (**PP**) is crossed with a white-flowered pea plant (**pp**). Which describes their offspring?
column15: All Pp, with light purple flowers
column16: Half PP with purple flowers and half pp with white flowers
column28: Punnett square: PP × pp → all four boxes are Pp. Pp plants have purple flowers because P is dominant, so the F1 is all purple. Light purple would be a blend, which doesn't happen with complete dominance, and a 3:1 ratio is what you get in the F2.
column29: The PP parent can only give P, and the pp parent can only give p.

column9: Mendel crossed purebred yellow-seed plants (**YY**) with purebred green-seed plants (**yy**). He then let the offspring of this cross self-pollinate. What phenotype ratio did he get in the next generation?
column28: YY × yy gives all Yy offspring (the F1), and they have yellow seeds. When the F1 plants self-pollinate, Yy × Yy → YY, Yy, Yy, yy. Three boxes are yellow (YY or Yy) and one is green (yy), so the F2 is 3 yellow : 1 green. This result showed Mendel that the green allele was hidden, not lost, in the F1. All yellow describes the F1, not the F2; 1 yellow : 1 green would need a yy parent; and 3 green : 1 yellow flips the dominant and recessive traits.
column29: First work out the genotype of the offspring of YY × yy. Then cross two of those offspring and count yellow against green.

column9: Put the steps for solving a Punnett square problem in order.
column14: Fill each box with one allele from the top and one allele from the side.
column15: Choose letters for the alleles: a capital letter for dominant and the same lowercase letter for recessive.
column16: Count the boxes to write the genotype ratio, phenotype ratio, and percents.
column17: Write each parent's genotype from the information in the problem.
column18: Write one parent's alleles across the top and the other parent's alleles down the side.
column28: First pick letters (capital = dominant, lowercase = recessive), then write each parent's genotype, set up the square with one parent across the top and the other down the side, fill each box with one allele from each parent, and finally count the boxes to get the ratios and percents.
column29: For each step, ask what you need to have done before you can do it. Which step needs nothing from the other steps?

column9: In fruit flies, a gray body (**G**) is dominant over an ebony (black) body (**g**). Jae crosses a **GG** fly with a **Gg** fly. What percent of the offspring are expected to be **heterozygous**? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: GG × Gg → GG, Gg, GG, Gg. Two of the 4 boxes are Gg (heterozygous) = 50%. Every fly is expected to have a gray body, but only half are expected to be heterozygous.
column29: Fill in the square, then count only the boxes with one G and one g.

column9: **G** is dominant over **g**. Which cross is expected to give a **1:1** phenotype ratio?
column28: Gg × gg → Gg, Gg, gg, gg: 2 dominant : 2 recessive, which is a 1:1 ratio. Gg × Gg gives 3:1, and GG × gg and GG × Gg give all dominant offspring.
column29: A 1:1 ratio means half show each phenotype. Which cross puts the recessive genotype in exactly half the boxes?

column9: In tomato plants, tall vines (**D**) are dominant over dwarf vines (**d**). Two heterozygous plants are crossed (**Dd × Dd**). What percent of the offspring are expected to have tall vines? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Dd × Dd → DD, Dd, Dd, dd. Three of the 4 boxes have at least one D, so 75% of the offspring are expected to have tall vines. Only the dd box (25%) is dwarf.
column29: Count every box that has at least one capital D.

column9: A pea plant has the genotype **TtGg**. Which list shows all four kinds of gametes (sex cells) it can make?
column28: Each gamete gets one allele for each gene: T or t, plus G or g. The four combinations are TG, Tg, tG, and tg. A gamete never carries two alleles of the same gene (Tt, TT), and a single letter would leave out one of the genes.
column29: Each sex cell carries one height allele and one color allele.

column9: In a monohybrid Punnett square (2 boxes by 2 boxes), each box counts as 1/4 (25%) of the expected offspring.
column28: True. The 4 boxes are equally likely, so each box is 1/4 = 25%. That's why you can count boxes and multiply by 25% to get a percent: a genotype that fills two boxes has a 2 × 25% = 50% chance, and three boxes = 75%.
column29: There are 4 equally likely boxes. What fraction of the total is one box?

column9: Which of Mendel's ideas says that the two alleles for a trait separate when gametes form, so each egg or sperm gets only one allele?
column28: The Law of Segregation says the two alleles for a trait separate during meiosis, so each egg or sperm gets just one. Independent assortment is about different traits being inherited separately, the Law of Dominance is about one allele hiding another, and the Rule of Unit Factors says each organism has two factors for each trait (today we call them alleles: two copies of the gene, one from each parent).
column29: Rule out the law about which allele shows and the rule that each organism has two factors for a trait. Of the two laws left, which one is about a single gene's pair of alleles?

column9: Mendel followed two traits at once: plant height (**T**/**t**) and seed color (**Y**/**y**). Which statement describes his **Law of Independent Assortment**?
column14: A dominant allele hides a recessive allele in a heterozygote
column15: The height and color alleles a plant got from one parent stay together
column16: The two alleles for one trait separate when gametes form
column17: A gamete's height allele doesn't affect which color allele it gets
column28: The Law of Independent Assortment says alleles for different traits are inherited independently: which height allele a gamete gets has nothing to do with which color allele it gets. That is why a dihybrid cross can give new combinations, like tall plants with green seeds. If the alleles from one parent stayed together, those new combinations could never appear. One allele hiding another is the Law of Dominance, and the two alleles of one trait separating is the Law of Segregation.
column29: Two of the choices describe Mendel's other laws. Of the two left, which one explains how a dihybrid cross can produce new combinations, like tall plants with green seeds?

column9: In sheep, white wool (**W**) is dominant over black wool (**w**). Two heterozygous white sheep (**Ww × Ww**) have a lamb. What is the chance that the lamb is **heterozygous**? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Ww × Ww → WW, Ww, Ww, ww. Two of the 4 boxes are Ww, so the chance of a heterozygous lamb is 50%. Don't count the WW box: it has white wool, but it is homozygous.
column29: Count only the boxes that have one W and one w.

column9: In rabbits, black fur (**B**) is dominant over white fur (**b**). Maya crosses a heterozygous black rabbit with a white rabbit (**Bb × bb**). The expected **genotype ratio** (Bb : bb) is ___.
column28: Punnett square: Bb × bb → Bb, Bb, bb, bb. That is 2 Bb : 2 bb, which simplifies to 1:1 (half black, half white).
column29: Fill in the four boxes and count Bb against bb.

column9: In pea plants, inflated pods (**I**) are dominant over constricted pods (**i**). What fraction of the offspring of **Ii × ii** are expected to have constricted pods?
column28: Punnett square: Ii × ii → Ii, Ii, ii, ii. Two of the 4 boxes are ii (constricted), so 1/2 of the offspring. 1/4 would come from Ii × Ii, and 0 would need a homozygous dominant parent.
column29: The ii parent can only give i. What can the Ii parent give?

column9: In mice, black fur (**B**) is dominant over brown fur (**b**). A **Bb** mouse is crossed with a **BB** mouse. Which statements about the expected offspring are true? Select all that apply.
column14: None of them should have brown fur.
column28: Bb × BB → BB, Bb, BB, Bb. Every pup gets a B from the BB parent, so none can be brown (bb). Half of the boxes are BB and half are Bb (heterozygous). About 1/4 brown would need two Bb parents, and only 2 of the 4 boxes are heterozygous, not 3.
column29: Draw the Punnett square first, then check each statement against the four boxes.

column9: A plant is heterozygous for a trait. What percent of the gametes (sex cells) it makes are expected to carry the recessive allele?
column28: A heterozygous plant (for example, Tt) has one dominant and one recessive allele. When they separate during meiosis, half of the gametes get T and half get t, so 50% carry the recessive allele.
column29: The plant has two different alleles, and each gamete gets only one of them.

column9: Wyatt crosses a tall pea plant of unknown genotype with a short plant (**tt**). Tall (**T**) is dominant. Of the 40 offspring, 21 are tall and 19 are short. What is the genotype of Wyatt's tall plant?
column17: It can't be known from this cross
column28: About half the offspring are short (tt). Each short plant got a t from the short parent and a t from Wyatt's plant, so his plant must carry t: it is Tt. A TT plant crossed with tt would give 100% tall offspring. The cross does answer the question; that's the point of a test cross.
column29: The short offspring are tt. Where did each of their t alleles come from?

column9: In pea plants, purple flowers (**P**) are dominant over white flowers (**p**). A purple-flowered plant had one white-flowered parent. Its genotype must be ___.
column28: A white-flowered parent is pp, so it could only give p. The plant is purple, so it must also have a P. Its genotype must be Pp. PP is impossible because one allele came from the white parent.
column29: What allele did the white parent have to pass on?

column9: Two pea plants are crossed. Out of 400 offspring, about 300 are tall and 100 are short (tall, **T**, is dominant). What were the parents' genotypes most likely?
column28: 300 tall : 100 short is a 3:1 ratio, which comes from two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt). Tt × tt would give about 1:1 (200 : 200), and TT × tt or TT × Tt would give all tall offspring.
column29: Simplify 300 : 100. Which cross gives that ratio in a Punnett square?

column9: Two pea plants that are heterozygous for both height and seed color are crossed (**TtYy × TtYy**). Tall (**T**) is dominant to short (**t**), and yellow seeds (**Y**) are dominant to green seeds (**y**). What phenotype ratio is expected?
column14: 1 tall yellow : 1 tall green : 1 short yellow : 1 short green
column15: 9 tall yellow : 3 tall green : 3 short yellow : 1 short green
column17: 9 tall green : 3 tall yellow : 3 short green : 1 short yellow
column28: TtYy × TtYy is the classic dihybrid cross. Split and multiply: Tt × Tt = 3 tall : 1 short, and Yy × Yy = 3 yellow : 1 green. Multiplying gives 9 tall yellow : 3 tall green : 3 short yellow : 1 short green. 1:1:1:1 comes from a dihybrid test cross, 3:1 is a one-trait result, and "9 tall green : 3 tall yellow" has the seed colors switched.
column29: Solve each trait by itself (3:1 and 3:1), then multiply. Which group should be the biggest?

column9: In pea plants, tall (**T**) is dominant to short (**t**), and green pods (**G**) are dominant to yellow pods (**g**). Two plants that are **TtGg** are crossed. Out of 16 offspring, how many are expected to be **tall with yellow pods**?
column28: Split and multiply: Tt × Tt → 3/4 tall; Gg × Gg → 1/4 yellow (gg). Tall and yellow = 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16, so 3 out of 16 offspring. In the 16-box Punnett square, 3 boxes are tall with gg (TTgg, Ttgg, Ttgg).
column29: Find the fraction that are tall and the fraction that have yellow (recessive) pods, then multiply.

column9: In pea plants, tall (**T**) is dominant to short (**t**), and green pods (**G**) are dominant to yellow pods (**g**). A **TtGg** plant is crossed with a **ttgg** plant. Out of 80 offspring, about how many are expected to be **short with green pods**?
column28: This is a dihybrid test cross. Split and multiply: Tt × tt → 1/2 short; Gg × gg → 1/2 green. Short and green = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, and 1/4 × 80 = 20. A dihybrid test cross gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio, so each of the four phenotypes is about 20 out of 80.
column29: Do each trait separately, multiply the two fractions, then take that fraction of 80.

column9: In guinea pigs, black fur (**B**) is dominant over white fur (**b**), and a rough coat (**R**) is dominant over a smooth coat (**r**). A white, rough male whose mother had a smooth coat is crossed with a black, rough female that is heterozygous for both traits. Out of 16 pups, how many are expected to be **white with a rough coat**?
column28: The male is white, so he is bb. He has a rough coat, but his smooth-coated mother (rr) could only give him r, so he is Rr: bbRr. The female is BbRr. Split and multiply: Bb × bb → 1/2 white (bb); Rr × Rr → 3/4 rough (RR or Rr). White and rough = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8, and 3/8 × 16 = 6 pups. Treating the male as RR gives 8, and treating him as smooth (rr) gives 4.
column29: First write both parents' genotypes. What allele must the male have gotten from his smooth-coated mother?

column9: In summer squash, white fruit (**W**) is dominant over yellow fruit (**w**), and disk-shaped fruit (**D**) is dominant over sphere-shaped fruit (**d**). A **WWDd** plant is crossed with a **WwDd** plant. What percent of the offspring are expected to have **yellow** fruit? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Look at fruit color by itself: WW × Ww → WW, Ww, WW, Ww. Every offspring gets a W from the WW parent, so none can be ww: 0% have yellow fruit. The shape alleles (Dd × Dd) don't change the color answer.
column29: Split the problem: what can WW × Ww make for fruit color? Ignore shape for this question.

column9: Saffron's parents are both heterozygous for a recessive trait (**Aa × Aa**). Their first two children both show the recessive trait. What is the chance that their third child will show the recessive trait?
column14: 0%, because they already had their recessive children
column28: Each child is a separate event, like a new coin flip. For Aa × Aa, one box in four is aa, so every child has a 25% chance of showing the recessive trait, no matter what happened with the first two. Parents don't 'use up' recessive children, and the pattern doesn't have to continue.
column29: Do the egg and sperm for the third child 'remember' what happened with the first two children?

column9: Jacob crosses his rose-comb rooster with single-comb hens (rose comb, **R**, is dominant over single comb, **r**). The first 3 chicks all have rose combs. What is the best conclusion about the rooster?
column14: He could still be Rr; 3 chicks are too few to tell
column15: He must be RR, since none of the chicks have single combs
column16: He is probably Rr, since rose comb is the dominant trait
column17: The hens probably carry a hidden rose-comb allele (R)
column28: This is a test cross, but with only 3 chicks. If the rooster were Rr, each chick would have a 1/2 chance of a rose comb, so getting 3 rose-comb chicks is like flipping heads 3 times in a row: unlikely, but it happens about 1 time in 8. The result fits RR but doesn't prove it, so Jacob needs more chicks. If many more chicks all have rose combs, RR becomes the best conclusion, and a single-comb chick would prove he is Rr. A dominant phenotype alone doesn't tell you his genotype, and the single-comb hens must be rr, so they can't carry R.
column29: If the rooster were Rr, what chance would each chick have of a rose comb? How often does a coin land heads 3 times in a row?

column9: **A** is dominant over **a**. Which crosses can produce offspring that show the **recessive** phenotype? Select all that apply.
column28: A recessive phenotype needs aa, so both parents must be able to pass on a. Aa × Aa (25% aa), Aa × aa (50% aa), and aa × aa (100% aa) all work. Any cross with an AA parent can't make aa, because that parent always passes on A.
column29: For an aa offspring, each parent must have at least one a to give.

column9: Addy's parents are both heterozygous for a recessive trait (**Hh × Hh**). What is the chance that their first **two** children **both** show the recessive trait? Answer in %, as a number like 12.5 (don't round to a whole number).
column28: For Hh × Hh, each child has a 1/4 chance of being hh. The two children are separate events, and both have to happen, so multiply: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 = 6.25%. Adding (1/4 + 1/4 = 50%) is the wrong rule here.
column29: Find the chance for one child, then use the 'split and multiply' idea: both events have to happen.

column9: In one of Mendel's experiments, round-seeded plants were allowed to self-pollinate. Their offspring had 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled seeds (round, **R**, is dominant over wrinkled, **r**). About how many of these 7,324 seeds were most likely **heterozygous (Rr)**?
column28: 5,474 : 1,850 is about 3:1 (5,474 ÷ 1,850 ≈ 2.96), so the round parent plants were most likely Rr. Rr × Rr → RR, Rr, Rr, rr, so about half of all the seeds should be Rr: 1/2 × 7,324 ≈ 3,660, about the same as 2 out of every 3 round seeds (2/3 × 5,474 ≈ 3,650). About 5,470 counts every round seed as Rr, but 1 in 3 round seeds is RR. About 2,740 treats RR and Rr as equally common among the round seeds, and about 1,830 is only one box out of four (the RR seeds).
column29: First use the data to work out the parent plants' genotype. Then ask: in their Punnett square, what fraction of the boxes are Rr?

column9: Wyatt correctly fills in a Punnett square for two **Bb** dogs (black, **B**, is dominant over white, **b**). He says, "Our dogs are having 4 puppies, so the litter will match my Punnett square exactly." Which response is best?
column14: He is wrong; each puppy is a separate chance, so the litter can differ
column15: He is right; a Punnett square gives the exact count in every litter
column16: He is right, since a litter of 4 matches the 4 boxes of the square
column17: He is wrong; the square shows the parents' genotypes, not the puppies'
column28: A Punnett square ratio is a probability for each offspring, not a guarantee. For Bb × Bb, each puppy has a 3/4 (75%) chance of being black, and each puppy is a new coin flip, so a litter of 4 could have 4, 3, 2, 1, or even 0 black puppies. Having 4 puppies and 4 boxes is just a coincidence of numbers; it doesn't make the litter follow the square. The boxes show the possible offspring, not the parents. The ratio shows up more closely in large numbers of offspring.
column29: Is a Punnett square a promise or a prediction? Think about flipping a coin just 4 times.

column9: Storm crosses two pea plants that are heterozygous for both seed shape and seed color (**RrYy × RrYy**). Round (**R**) is dominant to wrinkled (**r**), and yellow (**Y**) is dominant to green (**y**). Out of 320 seeds, about how many are expected to be **wrinkled and green**?
column28: Wrinkled and green is rryy. Split and multiply: Rr × Rr → 1/4 rr; Yy × Yy → 1/4 yy. Both = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, and 1/16 × 320 = 20 seeds. This is the '1' in the 9:3:3:1 ratio.
